> Mr Knifton,
>
> Thank you for confirming that, having read the points, you confirm that
> this is the correct position.
>
> Before the matter is closed, I would be grateful if I could clarify one
> important point about the scope of that confirmation, as I do not wish the
> correspondence to be capable of being interpreted more broadly than the
> searches actually undertaken.
>
> My understanding is that your confirmation means that *no records were
> found for William Buckler or Mary Doreen Williams on the specific current
> registration systems searched by your registration team*, and that the
> Medical Examiner Service itself has no predecessor records because that
> service did not exist at the time of either death. Correct as explained
> in my original email.
>
> It does *not*, however, mean that searches have established that no
> historical records ever existed in relation to either death, nor that all
> records formerly held by the South Glamorgan Health Authority or its
> constituent hospitals and services have been searched and found not to
> exist. Unless there is something I am misunderstanding? I want to be sure I
> don't overlook any traces of evidence.  Correct, this would be the Health
> Board (Cardiff & Vale or C&V) to determine if records still exist.
>
> In particular, as I understand the position you have confirmed, the
> following remain separate questions outside the scope of the current
> systems search:
>
>    - whether hospital records relating to William Buckler's admission and
>    death at Llandough Hospital on or about 29 May 1990 were created and, if
>    so, whether any survive with Cardiff and Vale University Health Board or an
>    archive; For C&V to confirm
>    - whether equivalent medical, hospital or health-authority records
>    relating to Mary Doreen Williams were created and, if so, where any
>    surviving records are held; For C&V to confirm
>    - whether either death was referred to a coroner or involved a
>    post-mortem, inquest or other separate investigation; For coroner’s
>    office to confirm
>    - whether any relevant records formerly held by the South Glamorgan
>    Health Authority were transferred to a successor body or archive; and For
>    C&V to confirm
>    - where records no longer survive, whether they were destroyed under
>    an applicable retention and disposal process. They would have been
>    completed many years ago but this would be for the responsible Health Body
>    to confirm.
>
> I appreciate that these matters may fall outside your office's remit and I
> am not asking you to undertake those searches yourself. I simply want to
> ensure that the documentary record accurately distinguishes *"no records
> found on the systems searched"* from *"no historical records ever existed
> or survive anywhere within the former health-authority system."*
>
> If that distinction is correct, I would be grateful for your confirmation.
> I will then pursue the surviving-record and archival questions with the
> appropriate successor bodies.
>
> Thank you again for your assistance.
>
> Kind regards,
>
> *Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)* *Royal Signals Cyber and Electronic
> Warfare Professional and Life Member*

>
> *I am writing to enquire whether any records or references are held in
> relation to the following historical deaths that occurred in the Cardiff &
> Vale / Llandough area: 1. William (Billy) Buckler    - Died at Llandough
> Hospital on or about 29 May 1990, aged 41    - Reported cause: heart attack
> 2. Mary Doreen Williams    - Born 10 August 1913    - Death registered
> March 1983, South Glamorgan (Vol 28, Page 3029) Although these pre-date the
> current Medical Examiner Service, I would be grateful if you could advise
> whether any legacy records, referrals, or related documentation exist, or
> direct me to the appropriate archive or department that may hold such
> information.*
>
>
>
> The All Wales Medical Examiner Service was introduced on a non-statutory
> basis in 2019. It operated across Wales to provide independent scrutiny of
> deaths that were not referred to a coroner so deaths in 1983 and 1990 would
> not apply in this case. The service became statutory on 9 September 2024,
> when the death certification reforms came into force in England and Wales.
> From that date, independent scrutiny by a Medical Examiner became a legal
> requirement before registration of all non-coronial deaths. Therefore, for
> deaths in 1983/1990, there would have been no Medical Examiner Service.
> Death certification would have been carried out by the attending doctor,
> with referrals made to the coroner where required under the rules that
> existed at the time. The Medical Examiner system only arrived many decades
> later.
>
>
>
> If both deaths occurred in Secondary Care, Hospitals do maintain records
> of deaths that occurred in their facilities, but these are not generally
> public records.
>
>
>
> The official legal record of a death is the death certificate registered
> with the local registrar and held by the General Register Office (GRO). In
> Wales, you can obtain copies of death certificates dating back before 1983
> if the death was registered.  Hospital medical records are usually retained
> under NHS records management policies and may still exist for deaths in
> 1983, but access is restricted because they contain confidential medical
> information.
>
>
>
> If you are researching a specific death from 1990 at Llandough Hospital,
> possible sources are:
>
>
>
>    1. Death certificate from the General Register Office.
>    2. Glamorgan Archives for historical NHS administrative records.
>    3. The relevant NHS body that inherited Llandough Hospital records,
>    now part of Cardiff and Vale University Health Board.
>    4. Coroner's records, if an inquest was held.
>
>
>
> In 1990, Llandough Hospital was still an NHS hospital managed through the
> local health authority system. This was under the South Glamorgan Health
> Authority, which was responsible for hospitals in the Cardiff and Vale area
> before NHS trusts were created in the early 1990s and now the Cardiff &
> Vale University Health Board.
>
>
>
> They can be contacted here:
>
>
>
> Health Records - Cardiff and Vale University Health Board
>  
>
>
>
> GP records are generally retained for a long period. Under current NHS
> records management guidance, GP records are typically kept for 10 years
> after a patient's death before being destroyed so these records would be
> out of scope.
>
>
>
> I have asked our registration team to search both patients and there are
> no records found for either patients due to the time elapsed.
>
>
>
> Further comments have been provided below in red for reference.
>
>
>
> I hope that this is an acceptable response.
>
>
>
> Yours sincerely,
>

Dear Mr Buckler,
Thank you for your email.
I note your request for further clarification regarding my decision in my capacity as Monitoring Officer.
The assessment I undertook was limited to considering whether the information provided disclosed evidence which, if established, could indicate a failure by the member to comply with the statutory Member’s Code of Conduct. As Monitoring Officer, I do not have formal investigatory powers equivalent to those of the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales and I am not required to undertake an investigation or obtain representations from a member before deciding whether there is sufficient basis for a referral to be made. My role at this stage is to consider whether the information presented discloses evidence of conduct that appears capable of amounting to a breach of the Code.
In reaching my view, I considered the information provided within your complaint, including the chronology you supplied regarding correspondence sent to Councillor Carroll between February and July 2026. The substance of the complaint was that you had not received substantive responses to a number of emails sent over that period.
For completeness, I considered whether the conduct alleged could potentially engage any of the principal obligations contained within the Member's Code of Conduct. These include requirements that members show respect and consideration for others, do not engage in bullying, harassment or discriminatory behaviour, do not bring their office or authority into disrepute, do not improperly use their position to confer an advantage or disadvantage on any person, and do not misuse Council resources or confidential information.
Whilst I appreciate that the absence of a response to correspondence may be frustrating, the information provided did not disclose evidence of disrespectful behaviour, bullying, harassment, misuse of position, misuse of Council resources, disclosure of confidential information, conduct bringing the office of member or the authority into disrepute, or any other behaviour which appeared capable of amounting to a breach of the Code. In reaching that view, I considered the nature of the conduct alleged, namely a failure to respond to correspondence, and whether that conduct engaged any provision of the Code.
It is important to note that the Member’s Code of Conduct does not impose a general obligation on elected members to respond to all correspondence received from members of the public, nor does it prescribe timescales within which responses must be provided. The Code is concerned with standards of conduct rather than the quality, adequacy or timeliness of constituency casework. Consequently, a decision not to respond, or not to respond in the manner sought by a correspondent, does not of itself constitute evidence of a breach of the Code.
Given that the information provided did not disclose evidence which appeared capable of amounting to a breach of the Code, I did not consider it necessary or proportionate to seek comments from Councillor Carroll before reaching that conclusion. My decision was therefore based upon the information contained within your complaint and whether that information, taken at its highest, indicated a potential breach of the Code warranting further action.
For completeness, any person is entitled to submit a complaint directly to the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales if they believe a member has failed to comply with the Member’s Code of Conduct. The Ombudsman is independent of the Council and is responsible for determining whether a complaint should be investigated and, if so, whether any further action is appropriate.
I trust this clarifies the basis of my decision. Having reviewed the information provided, my position remains that I have not identified evidence which would justify further action by me in my capacity as Monitoring Officer.
Yours sincerely,

Dear Mr Buckler

Thank you for your email. As the main contact for Freedom of Information, I have not seen your request previously but I will explain what I can in regards to your original request:

I am writing to enquire whether any records or references are held in relation to the following historical deaths that occurred in the Cardiff & Vale / Llandough area:

1. William (Billy) Buckler
   - Died at Llandough Hospital on or about 29 May 1990, aged 41
   - Reported cause: heart attack

2. Mary Doreen Williams
   - Born 10 August 1913
   - Death registered March 1983, South Glamorgan (Vol 28, Page 3029)

Although these pre-date the current Medical Examiner Service, I would be grateful if you could advise whether any legacy records, referrals, or related documentation exist, or direct me to the appropriate archive or department that may hold such information.

The All Wales Medical Examiner Service was introduced on a non-statutory basis in 2019. It operated across Wales to provide independent scrutiny of deaths that were not referred to a coroner so deaths in 1983 and 1990 would not apply in this case. The service became statutory on 9 September 2024, when the death certification reforms came into force in England and Wales. From that date, independent scrutiny by a Medical Examiner became a legal requirement before registration of all non-coronial deaths. Therefore, for deaths in 1983/1990, there would have been no Medical Examiner Service. Death certification would have been carried out by the attending doctor, with referrals made to the coroner where required under the rules that existed at the time. The Medical Examiner system only arrived many decades later.

If both deaths occurred in Secondary Care, Hospitals do maintain records of deaths that occurred in their facilities, but these are not generally public records.

The official legal record of a death is the death certificate registered with the local registrar and held by the General Register Office (GRO). In Wales, you can obtain copies of death certificates dating back before 1983 if the death was registered.  Hospital medical records are usually retained under NHS records management policies and may still exist for deaths in 1983, but access is restricted because they contain confidential medical information.

If you are researching a specific death from 1990 at Llandough Hospital, possible sources are:


  1.  Death certificate from the General Register Office.
  2.  Glamorgan Archives for historical NHS administrative records.
  3.  The relevant NHS body that inherited Llandough Hospital records, now part of Cardiff and Vale University Health Board.
  4.  Coroner's records, if an inquest was held.

In 1990, Llandough Hospital was still an NHS hospital managed through the local health authority system. This was under the South Glamorgan Health Authority, which was responsible for hospitals in the Cardiff and Vale area before NHS trusts were created in the early 1990s and now the Cardiff & Vale University Health Board.

They can be contacted here:

Health Records - Cardiff and Vale University Health Board 

GP records are generally retained for a long period. Under current NHS records management guidance, GP records are typically kept for 10 years after a patient's death before being destroyed so these records would be out of scope.

I have asked our registration team to search both patients and there are no records found for either patients due to the time elapsed.

Further comments have been provided below in red for reference.

I hope that this is an acceptable response.

Yours sincerely,

> The All Wales Medical Examiner Service was introduced on a non-statutory
> basis in 2019. It operated across Wales to provide independent scrutiny of
> deaths that were not referred to a coroner so deaths in 1983 and 1990 would
> not apply in this case. The service became statutory on 9 September 2024,
> when the death certification reforms came into force in England and Wales.
> From that date, independent scrutiny by a Medical Examiner became a legal
> requirement before registration of all non-coronial deaths. Therefore, for
> deaths in 1983/1990, there would have been no Medical Examiner Service.
> Death certification would have been carried out by the attending doctor,
> with referrals made to the coroner where required under the rules that
> existed at the time. The Medical Examiner system only arrived many decades
> later.
>
>
>
> If both deaths occurred in Secondary Care, Hospitals do maintain records
> of deaths that occurred in their facilities, but these are not generally
> public records.
>
>
>
> The official legal record of a death is the death certificate registered
> with the local registrar and held by the General Register Office (GRO). In
> Wales, you can obtain copies of death certificates dating back before 1983
> if the death was registered.  Hospital medical records are usually retained
> under NHS records management policies and may still exist for deaths in
> 1983, but access is restricted because they contain confidential medical
> information.
>
>
>
> If you are researching a specific death from 1990 at Llandough Hospital,
> possible sources are:
>
>
>
>    1. Death certificate from the General Register Office.
>    2. Glamorgan Archives for historical NHS administrative records.
>    3. The relevant NHS body that inherited Llandough Hospital records,
>    now part of Cardiff and Vale University Health Board.
>    4. Coroner's records, if an inquest was held.
>
>
>
> In 1990, Llandough Hospital was still an NHS hospital managed through the
> local health authority system. This was under the South Glamorgan Health
> Authority, which was responsible for hospitals in the Cardiff and Vale area
> before NHS trusts were created in the early 1990s and now the Cardiff &
> Vale University Health Board.

>

>

> <https://cavuhb.nhs.wales/our-services/health-records/>

>
>
> GP records are generally retained for a long period. Under current NHS
> records management guidance, GP records are typically kept for 10 years
> after a patient's death before being destroyed so these records would be
> out of scope.

> I have asked our registration team to search both patients and there are

Dear Mr Buckler

Thank you for your email. As the main contact for Freedom of Information, I have not seen your request previously but I will explain what I can in regards to your original request:

I am writing to enquire whether any records or references are held in relation to the following historical deaths that occurred in the Cardiff & Vale / Llandough area:

1. William (Billy) Buckler
   - Died at Llandough Hospital on or about 29 May 1990, aged 41
   - Reported cause: heart attack

2. Mary Doreen Williams
   - Born 10 August 1913
   - Death registered March 1983, South Glamorgan (Vol 28, Page 3029)

Although these pre-date the current Medical Examiner Service, I would be grateful if you could advise whether any legacy records, referrals, or related documentation exist, or direct me to the appropriate archive or department that may hold such information.

The All Wales Medical Examiner Service was introduced on a non-statutory basis in 2019. It operated across Wales to provide independent scrutiny of deaths that were not referred to a coroner so deaths in 1983 and 1990 would not apply in this case. The service became statutory on 9 September 2024, when the death certification reforms came into force in England and Wales. From that date, independent scrutiny by a Medical Examiner became a legal requirement before registration of all non-coronial deaths. Therefore, for deaths in 1983/1990, there would have been no Medical Examiner Service. Death certification would have been carried out by the attending doctor, with referrals made to the coroner where required under the rules that existed at the time. The Medical Examiner system only arrived many decades later.

If both deaths occurred in Secondary Care, Hospitals do maintain records of deaths that occurred in their facilities, but these are not generally public records.

The official legal record of a death is the death certificate registered with the local registrar and held by the General Register Office (GRO). In Wales, you can obtain copies of death certificates dating back before 1983 if the death was registered.  Hospital medical records are usually retained under NHS records management policies and may still exist for deaths in 1983, but access is restricted because they contain confidential medical information.

If you are researching a specific death from 1990 at Llandough Hospital, possible sources are:


  1.  Death certificate from the General Register Office.
  2.  Glamorgan Archives for historical NHS administrative records.
  3.  The relevant NHS body that inherited Llandough Hospital records, now part of Cardiff and Vale University Health Board.
  4.  Coroner's records, if an inquest was held.

In 1990, Llandough Hospital was still an NHS hospital managed through the local health authority system. This was under the South Glamorgan Health Authority, which was responsible for hospitals in the Cardiff and Vale area before NHS trusts were created in the early 1990s and now the Cardiff & Vale University Health Board.

texts.gm-1a032c58b0382b4c:
Dear Mr Buckler

Thank you for your email. As the main contact for Freedom of Information, I have not seen your request previously but I will explain what I can in regards to your original request:

I am writing to enquire whether any records or references are held in relation to the following historical deaths that occurred in the Cardiff & Vale / Llandough area:

1. William (Billy) Buckler
   - Died at Llandough Hospital on or about 29 May 1990, aged 41
   - Reported cause: heart attack

2. Mary Doreen Williams
   - Born 10 August 1913
   - Death registered March 1983, South Glamorgan (Vol 28, Page 3029)

Although these pre-date the current Medical Examiner Service, I would be grateful if you could advise whether any legacy records, referrals, or related documentation exist, or direct me to the appropriate archive or department that may hold such information.

The All Wales Medical Examiner Service was introduced on a non-statutory basis in 2019. It operated across Wales to provide independent scrutiny of deaths that were not referred to a coroner so deaths in 1983 and 1990 would not apply in this case. The service became statutory on 9 September 2024, when the death certification reforms came into force in England and Wales. From that date, independent scrutiny by a Medical Examiner became a legal requirement before registration of all non-coronial deaths. Therefore, for deaths in 1983/1990, there would have been no Medical Examiner Service. Death certification would have been carried out by the attending doctor, with referrals made to the coroner where required under the rules that existed at the time. The Medical Examiner system only arrived many decades later.

If both deaths occurred in Secondary Care, Hospitals do maintain records of deaths that occurred in their facilities, but these are not generally public records.

The official legal record of a death is the death certificate registered with the local registrar and held by the General Register Office (GRO). In Wales, you can obtain copies of death certificates dating back before 1983 if the death was registered.  Hospital medical records are usually retained under NHS records management policies and may still exist for deaths in 1983, but access is restricted because they contain confidential medical information.

If you are researching a specific death from 1990 at Llandough Hospital, possible sources are:


  1.  Death certificate from the General Register Office.
  2.  Glamorgan Archives for historical NHS administrative records.
  3.  The relevant NHS body that inherited Llandough Hospital records, now part of Cardiff and Vale University Health Board.
  4.  Coroner's records, if an inquest was held.

In 1990, Llandough Hospital was still an NHS hospital managed through the local health authority system. This was under the South Glamorgan Health Authority, which was responsible for hospitals in the Cardiff and Vale area before NHS trusts were created in the early 1990s and now the Cardiff & Vale University Health Board.

They can be contacted here:

Health Records - Cardiff and Vale University Health Board<https://cavuhb.nhs.wales/our-services/health-records/>

GP records are generally retained for a long period. Under current NHS records management guidance, GP records are typically kept for 10 years after a patient's death before being destroyed so these records would be out of scope.

I have asked our registration team to search both patients and there are no records found for either patients due to the time elapsed.

Further comments have been provided below in red for reference.

I hope that this is an acceptable response.

Yours sincerely,

Tim Knifton, MSc Gwybodeg Iechyd/Health Informatics
Rheolwr Rheoli Gwybodaeth/Information Governance Manager

(a) records which do not exist;

(b) records which once existed but have been destroyed;

I would be grateful for confirmation of the review and, where applicable, the relevant FOI reference number.

Glamorgan Archives Team,

I am writing to make a targeted archive research enquiry concerning the
DBDT collection and any related Bute, Mountjoy or Western Ground Rents
material held by Glamorgan Archives.

I am investigating the historic title, occupation and parcel
boundaries of *Great
House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough*, particularly evidence concerning a
possible historical division of the farm between land retained by the Bute
Estate and land allegedly sold or transferred to *Daniel Thomas*.

A family witness account describes a specific arrangement under which
approximately ten acres, including the farmhouse, were allegedly sold by
the Bute Estate to Daniel Thomas, while a separate portion of approximately
nine acres remained under the Bute Estate. The account further describes
quarrying on the Thomas-held land and an agreement under which the freehold
would eventually pass to the occupying family when quarrying ceased.

I appreciate that this account requires verification against the original
documentary record. I am therefore seeking to identify the relevant deeds,
agreements, plans and subsequent title documents.
1. Verification of specific DBDT catalogue entries

Please confirm the exact property description, parties and date of the
following catalogue entries, and, if possible, provide a digital copy or
scan of the opening parties clause and any attached or marginal plan:

   -

   *DBDT10/19* – Lease (counterpart), described in the catalogue as
   concerning land and messuages in Bute Street, Cardiff, from trustees of the
   late Marquess of Bute to Mr Daniel Thomas, October 1850.
   -

   *DBDT10/20* – Agreement for a building lease of premises in Bute Town,
   Cardiff, involving the same parties, June 1849.

I understand from the catalogue descriptions that these items concern
Cardiff rather than Llandough. My purpose is to establish whether the *Daniel
Thomas named in these instruments can be identified sufficiently to
determine whether he is the same individual later connected with the
Llandough lime works and land interests*, or whether these are unrelated
transactions involving another person of the same name.

Please also advise whether either document contains information identifying
Daniel Thomas by residence, occupation, estate, trusteeship or other
distinguishing details.
2. Targeted search for a Bute–Daniel Thomas transaction at or near Llandough

Please search the catalogue descriptions and indexes available to Glamorgan
Archives for any deed, conveyance, exchange, sale, transfer, lease,
agreement, plan or related instrument involving:

   - *Daniel Thomas*;
   - *Alfred Thomas*;
   - the *Marquess of Bute*;
   - trustees of the Marquess of Bute;
   - the *Bute Estate*;

and land at or near:

   - *Llandough*;
   - *Great House Farm / Great House / Tŷ Mawr*;
   - adjoining land or parcels that may subsequently have formed part of
   the farm.

I am particularly interested in transactions dating from approximately *1876
to 1878*, but would be grateful for references to earlier or later
documents where they form part of the same chain of title.

In particular, I am seeking evidence capable of confirming or disproving
whether any defined parcel of land was conveyed by the Bute Estate to
Daniel Thomas.
3. Quarrying, lime works and any conditional reversion or transfer

Please identify any relevant records concerning land at Llandough or Great
House Farm that refer to:

   - quarrying;
   - quarries or quarry land;
   - lime works or lime kilns;
   - mineral rights;
   - removal of quarrying machinery;
   - reduction or cessation of rent as land was quarried;
   - termination of quarrying;
   - a future conveyance, reversion, surrender or transfer of a freehold
   interest when quarrying ceased.

The particular issue I am investigating is whether an agreement existed
under which occupation or ownership of a defined parcel was intended to
change when quarrying operations came to an end.
4. Daniel Thomas, Alfred Thomas and the Llandough lime works

Please identify any documents linking *Daniel Thomas*, or his son *Alfred
Thomas (later Lord Pontypridd)*, with:

   - land at Llandough;
   - the Llandough lime works or lime kilns;
   - quarrying operations;
   - Great House Farm or adjoining agricultural land;
   - any freehold or leasehold interest in the area.

I would be particularly interested in estate papers, correspondence,
conveyances, wills, probate-related estate records, rentals, rent books,
abstracts of title and plans that may trace what became of any Daniel
Thomas interest after his death or thereafter.
5. Subsequent title and occupation

Please identify any abstracts of title, estate maps, conveyances,
correspondence, tenancy records or other material that may assist in
establishing:

   1. what happened to any freehold interest held by Daniel Thomas or his
   estate;
   2. whether such an interest was ever conveyed, surrendered or
   transferred back to the Bute Estate or another party;
   3. whether the Bute Estate later reacquired any relevant parcel;
   4. whether later parties, including *Mountjoy Ltd* or *Western Ground
   Rents Ltd*, acquired title to land previously held by Daniel Thomas or
   his successors;
   5. the basis on which later tenancies described as covering the "whole"
   of Great House Farm were granted.

I am also interested in any material linking these title questions with the
occupation of the farm by the *Williams family*.
6. Plans and parcel boundaries

A separate line of research concerns the possibility that historic legal
boundaries passed through or between different parts of the Great House
Farm complex.

Accordingly, please identify any:

   - estate maps;
   - conveyance plans;
   - tenancy plans;
   - quarry plans;
   - large-scale plans;
   - boundary plans;
   - valuation plans;

that show Great House Farm, the farmhouse, garden, stables, outbuildings or
adjoining parcels.

I am particularly interested in documents that could establish whether
different parts of the historic building complex fell within different
legal parcels.

I appreciate that some of these requests may require staff research beyond
a standard enquiry. My immediate priority is to obtain *the relevant
catalogue references and confirmation of what material exists*. If more
detailed searching or document retrieval is necessary, please let me know
the applicable procedure, estimated cost and whether a formal paid research
request would be required.

If relevant documents have been digitised, I would be grateful for details
of the cost of obtaining copies. Otherwise, please advise whether they can
be consulted in person and whether any restrictions or advance ordering
requirements apply.

Thank you for your assistance. The documents identified through this
enquiry may be important to reconstructing the historical chain of title
and occupation of Great House Farm, Llandough from the nineteenth century
onwards.

Yours faithfully,

*Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)*

Dear Bev,

Thank you for checking the system and for your prompt and helpful reply.

I am grateful for the clarification regarding the historical position of
Cardiff and Vale cases prior to 2002, and I will now pursue enquiries with
Glamorgan Archives.

Before I do so, I would be grateful if I could clarify one point concerning
the result of your search, particularly in relation to my grandmother, Mary
Doreen Williams.

My purpose is not simply genealogical. I am attempting to reconstruct and
forensically assess the historical circumstances surrounding her death in
1983, and there is information concerning the circumstances before and
around her death which I am seeking to reconcile against the surviving
official documentary record.

Could you therefore please confirm whether your statement that you are
"unable to locate any details" means only that neither individual appears
in the records or computerised/indexed system currently available to your
office, or whether your office is able positively to state that neither
death was ever referred to the coroner?

In particular, if you are able to clarify, I would be grateful to know
whether the absence of a record in your system excludes, or does not
exclude, the historical existence of:

   - a report of the death to a coroner;
   - a preliminary coroner's enquiry;
   - a post-mortem examination;
   - an inquest;
   - correspondence with the police, hospital or other authority;
   - a case file or register subsequently transferred to an archive or
   destroyed in accordance with an applicable retention policy.

I appreciate that you may not hold the historical records themselves. I am
not asking you to speculate about the circumstances of either death. I am
simply seeking to ensure that I correctly understand the evidential
significance of the negative search result before proceeding to the archive.

If possible, I would also be grateful if you could confirm the name of the
coroner jurisdiction or office responsible for Llandough/Llandough Hospital
in March 1983, when Mary Doreen Williams died, and whether you know which
body would have inherited or transferred that jurisdiction's surviving
records.

For completeness, if there are any records held off-system, legacy indexes,
paper registers, accession records or transfer information which are not
searchable through the system you checked, I would be grateful if you could
let me know whether those exist and who now holds them.

I appreciate your assistance. I am trying to establish the documentary
facts carefully and avoid drawing conclusions before the relevant records
have been located or ruled out.

Kind regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

Sir/Madam,

I write to give formal notice of documentary evidence which, if correctly
understood, raises a potentially material question concerning the
historical identity, ownership and/or title to land formerly known as *Great
House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough*, subsequently developed for residential
purposes including *Church View Close*.

This correspondence is intended as a *governance and integrity notification*.
It is not an FOI or EIR request, nor am I asking the Council at this stage
to accept my allegations or conclusions as established fact.
1. The land and subsequent development

The land concerned is the former Great House Farm / Ty Mawr site at
Llandough.

The site was subsequently developed for residential use. Planning and
associated administrative decisions were therefore made in circumstances in
which ownership of the relevant land appears to have been treated as
sufficiently established for those purposes.

I am notifying the Council because documentary evidence now assembled
appears to raise a material question as to whether the historical title
position was in fact conclusively established, and whether that question
was adequately identified, examined and recorded within the Council's
administrative and planning records.
2. Potential title-chain discrepancy

The documentary record presently available to me indicates a historical
dispute concerning the land involving my grandmother and the
Williams/Buckler family on one side and BP-related entities on the other.

My understanding of the available records is that:

   - proceedings in 1974 did not result in a final judicial determination
   conclusively establishing the underlying title in the manner subsequently
   assumed;
   - a further hearing listed for *31 October 1974* did not proceed
   substantively;
   - the land was subsequently registered in the name of BP-related
   entities around *1982*;
   - my grandmother died in *1983*, without, on the evidence presently
   available to me, a final judicial determination of the underlying ownership
   dispute or compensation resolving the family's claim;
   - the subsequent *1987 Court of Appeal proceedings, BP Properties Ltd v
   Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2*, did not, in my assessment, constitute a
   comprehensive adjudication of every underlying historical title question
   now arising from the documentary record.

I emphasise that I am *not asking the Council to determine the civil title
itself*. Rather, I am asking whether the Council has properly established
what was actually determined by the courts, what remained disputed, what
documentary basis was relied upon for treating title as settled, and
whether that distinction was properly reflected in its own records and
decision-making.

That distinction is important.
3. Documentary evidence

I have assembled documentary material concerning the historical title
chain, court proceedings, registration history, conveyances and associated
records, together with a chronological record of notifications and
responses.

The core documentary evidence can be supplied to the Council immediately.

Some of the underlying material and references have also been raised in
previous correspondence with the Council and other public bodies. I
therefore request that this notification be considered alongside the
relevant material already held on Council files, rather than treated as an
isolated new allegation.
4. Authorities previously notified

The matter has previously been raised with, among others:

   - the Planning Department — from 31 January 2026 and subsequently;
   - the Council's FOI / Information Governance function, including case
   *00210772*;
   - Councillor George Carroll — through multiple contacts between February
   and July 2026;
   - Corporate Complaints / the Monitoring Officer — including
   correspondence dated 27 July 2026 and the determination dated 12 August
   2026;
   - Cadw and the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments
   of Wales (RCAHMW);
   - other public bodies involved in the continuing documentary and
   evidential trail.

I am concerned that the substantive governance question identified above
has not yet been independently addressed.
5. Matters requiring independent examination

In particular, I request that the Council establish:

   1.

   *Whether the historical title dispute was ever conclusively determined
   by a competent court*, distinguishing between orders concerning
   possession, proceedings concerning particular issues, and an actual final
   determination of the underlying title.
   2.

   *What documentary evidence the Council historically relied upon when
   treating ownership of the relevant land as established* for planning,
   development, conveyancing or other administrative purposes.
   3.

   *Whether the Council's planning and administrative records contain any
   recognition of the historical dispute*, including any consideration of
   competing title claims or unresolved matters affecting the identity or
   ownership of the land.
   4.

   *Whether any independent review of these issues has previously been
   undertaken*, and if so, by whom, on what terms, and with what
   conclusions.
   5.

   *Whether any current Council officer involved in reviewing this
   notification has previously participated materially in the decisions,
   complaints, correspondence or investigations now under examination*,
   and, if so, what arrangements will be made to ensure genuine independence.
   6.

   *Whether the Council considers that any governance, record-keeping,
   planning or public-confidence issue remains outstanding*, irrespective
   of the ultimate determination of civil title.

6. Why independent examination is warranted

The fact that the land has subsequently been developed does not, by itself,
resolve the historical documentary question.

If the evidence demonstrates that a material title issue was overlooked,
misunderstood or inadequately recorded, that may have implications
extending beyond the original ownership dispute, including the accuracy and
integrity of public records and the basis upon which subsequent
administrative decisions were made.

Conversely, if the Council considers that the historical record
conclusively resolves the matter, I ask that it identify *the specific
documentary and judicial basis for that conclusion*.

That is why I am requesting an independent examination rather than asking
individual officers who have previously dealt with the matter simply to
reaffirm earlier positions.
7. Formal request

I therefore formally request that the Council:

*a.* acknowledge this notification and identify the officer or function
responsible for independently reviewing it;

*b.* confirm how that review will be kept independent of officers who have
previously dealt substantively with the matter;

*c.* identify the principal Council records and documentary evidence that
will be considered;

*d.* determine whether the historical title issue described above has
previously been properly examined and recorded;

*e.* identify any material governance or administrative issue that remains
outstanding; and

*f.* provide a written response setting out the process to be followed and
the anticipated timescale.

For the avoidance of doubt, I am *not asking the Council to accept that
fraud, unlawful dispossession or defective title has been established*. I
am notifying the Council that documentary evidence appears to raise a
potentially material question concerning the historical identity and/or
title to land upon which subsequent development took place, and I am asking
the Council to establish whether that question has ever been properly
examined.

If the Council considers that determination of the underlying civil title
falls outside its functions, I would nevertheless ask it to address the
separate governance question: *whether its own historical records and
decision-making properly identified and dealt with the title issue on the
evidence available to it.*

This is a *formal governance and integrity notification*, not an FOI or EIR
request.

I would be grateful for written acknowledgement and confirmation of the
process and timescale for an independent determination.

Yours sincerely,

*Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)*

Dear Ret'd Sergeant Sion Buckler,



Thank you for your enquiry of 13/08/2026 regarding a review of:



We are handling your request under the Freedom of Information Act 2000.



From our initial assessment it is clear that we will not be able to answer your request without further clarification. Under section 1(3) of the Act, a public authority need not comply with a request unless any further information reasonably required to locate the information is supplied.



In order to progress your request, we require clarification on the scope of your request.



The FOI Centre has received a request for the following:



My request was deliberately framed more broadly than a simple catalogue search for the words “Great House Farm”, “Ty Mawr”, “Llandough” or “Cedfin”. I specifically asked The National Archives to identify recorded information concerning the existence, transfer, retention, destruction, disposal or absence of records, including records that might not be catalogued under the property's later or local names.



Your response confirms only that you searched the PRO and RW series using:



“Great House Farm” OR “Ty Mawr” OR Llandough OR Cedfin



combined with “Glamorgan”, and that this produced no catalogue results.



You also correctly state that Discovery searches catalogue titles and descriptions rather than the contents of records. That qualification is important, because it means the search described cannot establish that relevant records did not exist, were never transferred, or were destroyed.



In particular, your response does not appear to address the other categories expressly identified in my request, including searches or recorded information relating to:



  *   Western Ground Rents Ltd;

  *   BP Pension Trust Ltd;

  *   BP Properties Ltd;

  *   Mountjoy Ltd;

  *   the proceedings in BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2;

  *   the 1982–1983 registration and associated government or administrative records;

  *   the 1980–1988 public campaign and governmental correspondence;

  *   the 1988 eviction and demolition;

  *   Cadw or central-government communications concerning the property;

  *   European Commission of Human Rights Application 14464/88;

  *   records concerning transfer, destruction or disposal of potentially relevant material; and

  *   HMC9/311 or related archival references.



These alternative lines of enquiry are intentional. The purpose is to establish whether relevant information can be identified through the government bodies, corporate entities, court proceedings, administrative processes and archival transfers associated with the property, rather than relying solely upon the modern name by which the property is known.



I am conducting corresponding enquiries with other repositories and public bodies. This is specifically intended to triangulate the documentary history where records may have been catalogued under a different creator, department, legal proceeding, estate, corporate body or administrative function.



I therefore ask that you do not treat the absence of a Discovery keyword hit as an answer to the substantive questions raised.



Please clarify:



  1.  Whether the searches undertaken were limited to the PRO and RW catalogue series and the four property/location search terms identified in your email.



  1.  Whether The National Archives searched for the named corporate bodies, court proceedings and application references identified in my request, rather than only searching the property names.



  1.  Whether The National Archives holds any recorded transfer, accession, disposal, destruction or retention information indicating that records concerning the relevant property, estate, companies, litigation or government involvement were transferred elsewhere, destroyed, or otherwise disposed of.



  1.  If such information is not held, whether this is because no such records are held, because no relevant records were ever transferred to TNA, or because TNA's catalogue/search systems contain no discoverable description of them.



  1.  Whether HMC9/311 or related series have been checked, or whether that reference falls outside the search undertaken.



  1.  Whether there are central-government, court, departmental or administrative records relating to the litigation and entities identified above which may contain references to the property without using “Great House Farm”, “Ty Mawr”, “Llandough” or “Cedfin” in the catalogue description.



For the avoidance of doubt, I am not asking The National Archives to infer the contents of uncatalogued records or to undertake an unlimited research project. I am asking for confirmation of the recorded information held by TNA concerning the existence, provenance, transfer, retention, destruction or disposal of potentially relevant records, and for the searches undertaken to locate that information.



That distinction is particularly important because a catalogue search returning no result is not equivalent to a finding that no relevant historical, governmental or archival records existed.



I would therefore be grateful if this could be reconsidered as a response to the scope of the original FOI enquiry rather than treated solely as a request for assistance with a Discovery keyword search.



I am continuing parallel enquiries with the National Library of Wales, Glamorgan Archives, Cadw, RCAHMW, HM Land Registry and other relevant bodies. The purpose of these enquiries is to establish the documentary chain independently and to identify where records were created, transferred, retained or potentially destroyed.



An acknowledgment email was sent on 17/08/2026, informing you we are handling your request under the FOI Act and that the request has been given a reference number: CAS-347296-M0V4Y1.



Today (20/08/2026) we have received the following:



I wrote to you on 12 August 2026 with a follow-up refining my earlier enquiry concerning National Farm Survey / MAFF records relating to Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan (Williams / Buckler family interest).



I have not yet received a substantive reply to that follow-up and would be grateful for an update on progress and the expected timescale for a full response.

BP Archive Team,

I am writing to enquire about records held within the BP corporate archive relating to the former Great House Farm / Ty Mawr property at Llandough, near Penarth, Glamorgan, South Wales.

I am conducting historical and legal research into the property, which was acquired by BP Pension Trust Ltd in December 1969 and subsequently administered by BP Properties Ltd. The property was the subject of extensive litigation, including BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, followed by the eviction of the occupying family in 1988 and demolition of the farmhouse later that year.

Research context

The central issue of my research is the identification of the individual parcels comprising the historic property.

The evidence currently being examined indicates that the historic complex may have comprised separately identifiable:

  *   a house-and-garden plot;
  *   a western agricultural/farm plot containing the barn, stables and courtyard; and
  *   an eastern cottages plot.

Later mapping and Land Registry records appear to have treated some of these areas as a combined property.

I am therefore particularly interested in establishing what BP itself understood the boundaries and constituent parcels of the property to be, and when any change or consolidation of those parcels occurred.

Records sought

I would be grateful if the BP Archive could search its holdings for records concerning:

  *   BP Properties Ltd;
  *   BP Pension Trust Ltd;
  *   British Petroleum and relevant predecessor/subsidiary property records;
  *   Great House Farm / Great House / Ty Mawr, Llandough;
  *   Llandough-juxta-Penarth / Cogan / Penarth;
  *   the Williams and Buckler families;
  *   possession proceedings and enforcement, particularly 1955, 1962 and 1974-1988;
  *   property acquisition, title investigation and disposal;
  *   conveyances, title deeds, abstracts of title and schedules of deeds;
  *   estate-management correspondence;
  *   property, site and boundary plans;
  *   Land Registry correspondence and registration, particularly 1982-1983.

The relevant period is approximately 1955-1988, with particular emphasis on 1962-1983.

Three priority categories

If relevant material survives, I would particularly like to identify the following, in this order:

1. The BP Properties Ltd / BP Pension Trust Ltd property file for Great House Farm / Ty Mawr, Llandough

In particular, any acquisition/title file containing the original property description, conveyances, title investigation, schedules of deeds, property plans, boundary plans or correspondence identifying exactly which land and buildings BP considered to form the property.

2. The legal/property file relating to the 1962 possession proceedings and subsequent enforcement/re-entry

In particular, any BP legal correspondence, instructions to solicitors, plans, property descriptions or internal documents identifying the land and buildings to which the possession order was understood to apply.

3. The 1982-1983 title/registration/consolidation file

In particular, correspondence, plans, conveyances, title investigation and Land Registry material concerning the registration or amalgamation of the relevant parcels, including any documentation showing how the house-and-garden, eastern cottages and western farm/barn/stables/courtyard areas were treated.

If these exact files do not survive, I would be very grateful for the nearest surviving files, alternative references or catalogue entries covering the same transactions.

Access

I would also appreciate advice on:

  *   whether the relevant records are available for public research;
  *   whether they can be viewed in person at the BP Archive at the University of Warwick;
  *   whether advance appointment or reader registration is required;
  *   whether particular records require advance retrieval;
  *   whether copies or digital reproductions can be ordered; and
  *   whether any relevant records are subject to closure or other access restrictions.

I am happy to provide further information, including the relevant court case reference, property names, dates and Land Registry title numbers, if this would assist the archivist in identifying the records.

Research purpose

I am particularly interested in contemporary BP documentation rather than later summaries, because the central research question is what BP itself understood the property's legal identity, boundaries and constituent parcels to be at the relevant dates.

Thank you very much for any assistance you can provide.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler

FOI Team,

Thank you for your detailed response and for undertaking the additional
enquiries.

I appreciate the further information you have provided concerning the
searches undertaken. However, I would like to request an internal review
under the Freedom of Information Act 2000.

My concern is not simply that no objects have been identified. It is
whether the searches undertaken have fully addressed the scope of my
original request, particularly the documentary evidence concerning the
provenance, acquisition, transfer, ownership, identification and dispersal
of material originating from Great House Farm (Ty Mawr).

I would be grateful if the internal review could consider the following
points.

*1. Information identified concerning Great House Farm*

Your response states that the additional enquiries identified “some
information relating generally to Great House Farm and the surrounding
area”.

Please could you identify what categories of information this refers to
and, where it is not exempt, provide the relevant recorded information or
explain where it can be accessed?

This appears potentially relevant to the original request even if it does
not itself identify furniture or household objects.

*2. Scope of the archived electronic search*

You state that the Information Technology team reviewed “archived
electronic systems and records retained by the Museum”.

Please could the review clarify:

   - which archived systems were searched;
   - the approximate date ranges covered;
   - whether historical email or correspondence archives were searched;
   - whether legacy collections-management databases were searched;
   - whether databases or systems preceding the current CMS were searched;
   and
   - whether any archived systems were unavailable, incomplete or incapable
   of being searched.

*3. Correspondence and administrative records*

My original request expressly sought correspondence concerning the
identification, recovery, ownership or location of objects, as well as
correspondence with the Bute Estate, Cardiff Council, Cardiff Castle and
other public authorities.

Your response refers generally to “associated collection documentation” and
“administrative records”, but does not make clear whether historical
correspondence files were specifically searched.

Please could the internal review establish whether searches were made of:

   - curator correspondence;
   - departmental correspondence files;
   - donor correspondence;
   - acquisition correspondence;
   - disposal correspondence;
   - loan correspondence;
   - provenance correspondence;
   - correspondence with Cardiff Council;
   - correspondence with Cardiff Castle;
   - correspondence with the Bute Estate;
   - correspondence with other museums or public authorities; and
   - any relevant institutional or external correspondence indexes.

*4. Search terms*

Thank you for identifying many of the search terms used.

Please could the internal review confirm whether the search also included
combinations and variants involving:

   - “Bute Estate”
   - “Bute”
   - “Cardiff Castle”
   - “Cardiff Council”
   - “Great House Farm”
   - “Ty Mawr”
   - “Great House”
   - “Llandough”
   - “Buckler”
   - “Williams”
   - “Mary Williams”
   - “Mary Doreen Williams”
   - “household effects”
   - “contents”
   - “furniture”
   - “furnishings”
   - “heirlooms”
   - “fixtures”
   - “estate”
   - “dispersal”
   - “recovery”
   - “provenance”
   - “ownership”
   - “transfer”
   - “demolition”

I appreciate that historical records may not have been consistently
indexed, which is why I would be grateful for confirmation of the
methodology used.

*5. Transfer, disposal and destruction*

Your response states:

“We are also not aware of any relevant collection records relating to such
material having been transferred to another institution or destroyed.”

Please could the internal review clarify whether this conclusion is based
upon:

a. a search of transfer/accession-out records;

b. a review of retention and disposal records;

c. enquiries with relevant collections staff;

d. review of archival transfer documentation; or

e. institutional knowledge rather than a documentary search.

I am particularly interested in distinguishing between “no record exists”
and “no record was identified in the systems searched”.

*6. The original request concerning external institutions*

The original request was deliberately framed broadly because the question
concerns possible dispersal of the contents of a demolished historic
property.

It expressly included records concerning Cardiff Council, Cardiff Castle,
the Bute Estate, museums, Arts Council England, DCMS, RCEWA and other
public authorities.

I would therefore be grateful if the review could confirm whether records
of communications or transactions involving those bodies were searched
within Amgueddfa Cymru's records, rather than simply searching the Museum's
object catalogue for Great House Farm objects.

*7. Advice and assistance*

You have stated that Cardiff Council and Cardiff Castle “would appear to be
the organisations most likely to hold records relating to furniture,
furnishings or other movable property associated with Great House Farm”.

I appreciate that you cannot transfer another authority's records to me.
However, could you please provide any further information available to the
Museum as to *which particular department, collection, archive or record
series at Cardiff Council or Cardiff Castle is most likely to contain such
material*?

That would materially assist me in directing subsequent FOI and archival
enquiries.

I am grateful for the additional work already undertaken. I am requesting
the internal review because I would like the record to be clear as to
precisely what was searched, what information was identified, and what the
negative result does and does not establish.

I am not asking Amgueddfa Cymru to determine any allegation concerning the
historical ownership of Great House Farm. The purpose of the review is
simply to ensure that the documentary search corresponds fully with the
scope of the original FOI request.

Please treat this email as my formal request for an internal review of FOI
2026-020.

Regards,


Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

Thank you for your response.

I accept the distinction you draw between the Council's Corporate Concerns
and Complaints Policy and the separate statutory framework governing the
conduct of elected members. I am not seeking to use the corporate
complaints procedure as an appeal against historic planning, enforcement,
land or judicial decisions.

However, I do wish to clarify one important point concerning your decision
in your capacity as Monitoring Officer.

My complaint about Councillor George Carroll was not simply that the
Council should revisit historic decisions concerning Great House Farm. The
specific concern was his repeated failure to provide any substantive
response to correspondence sent to him in his capacity as the elected
councillor for Llandough, despite repeated approaches over a period of
approximately five months and despite the correspondence setting out
specific matters concerning his ward.

The chronology supplied with my complaint records correspondence on:

   - 16 February 2026;
   - 4 May 2026;
   - 7 June 2026;
   - 25 June 2026; and
   - 13 July 2026.

My complaint therefore concerned the conduct and handling of that
correspondence by an elected member, rather than asking the Monitoring
Officer to determine the underlying historical ownership or planning
dispute.

You state:

“Having reviewed the information you have provided, I have not identified
evidence which would indicate a breach of the Members Code of Conduct.”

I would therefore be grateful for clarification of the basis upon which
that conclusion was reached.

In particular, please confirm:

   1.

   *Which specific provisions of the Members' Code of Conduct were
   considered* in assessing my complaint.
   2.

   *Whether the complete correspondence chronology and the underlying
   emails and attachments were considered*, rather than merely my summary
   of them.
   3.

   *Whether Councillor Carroll was invited to provide an explanation or
   response* concerning the repeated absence of any substantive response to
   the correspondence.
   4.

   If so, whether his response was taken into account in reaching your
   conclusion.
   5.

   If not, please explain how the Monitoring Officer was able to determine
   that there was no evidence indicating a possible breach without obtaining
   the member's account of the conduct complained of.
   6.

   Please explain, in sufficient detail to enable me to understand the
   decision, *why the documented pattern of conduct was considered
   incapable of engaging any provision of the Members' Code of Conduct*.

necessarily constitute a breach of the Code. I am not asserting that

reached a definitive conclusion without identifying the relevant Code
provisions, the evidence considered, or the reasoning by which that
evidence was found insufficient.

instead be referred to the *Public Services Ombudsman for Wales* for

with my original complaint and the complete correspondence record, for
consideration of whether a complaint should be submitted to the Public
Services Ombudsman for Wales.

member.

Sarah Abbott,

Thank you for your response.

I have considered it carefully. Unfortunately, it does not appear to answer
the FOI enquiry I submitted.

My request was deliberately framed more broadly than a simple catalogue
search for the words “Great House Farm”, “Ty Mawr”, “Llandough” or
“Cedfin”. I specifically asked The National Archives to identify recorded
information concerning the *existence, transfer, retention, destruction,
disposal or absence of records*, including records that might not be
catalogued under the property's later or local names.

Your response confirms only that you searched the PRO and RW series using:

“Great House Farm” OR “Ty Mawr” OR Llandough OR Cedfin

combined with “Glamorgan”, and that this produced no catalogue results.

You also correctly state that Discovery searches catalogue titles and
descriptions rather than the contents of records. That qualification is
important, because it means the search described cannot establish that
relevant records did not exist, were never transferred, or were destroyed.

In particular, your response does not appear to address the other
categories expressly identified in my request, including searches or
recorded information relating to:

   - Western Ground Rents Ltd;
   - BP Pension Trust Ltd;
   - BP Properties Ltd;
   - Mountjoy Ltd;
   - the proceedings in *BP Properties Ltd v Buckler* [1987] EWCA Civ 2;
   - the 1982–1983 registration and associated government or administrative
   records;
   - the 1980–1988 public campaign and governmental correspondence;
   - the 1988 eviction and demolition;
   - Cadw or central-government communications concerning the property;
   - European Commission of Human Rights Application 14464/88;
   - records concerning transfer, destruction or disposal of potentially
   relevant material; and
   - HMC9/311 or related archival references.

These alternative lines of enquiry are intentional. The purpose is to
establish whether relevant information can be identified through the
*government
bodies, corporate entities, court proceedings, administrative processes and
archival transfers associated with the property*, rather than relying
solely upon the modern name by which the property is known.

I am conducting corresponding enquiries with other repositories and public
bodies. This is specifically intended to triangulate the documentary
history where records may have been catalogued under a different creator,
department, legal proceeding, estate, corporate body or administrative
function.

I therefore ask that you do not treat the absence of a Discovery keyword
hit as an answer to the substantive questions raised.

Please clarify:

   1.

   *Whether the searches undertaken were limited to the PRO and RW
   catalogue series and the four property/location search terms identified in
   your email.*
   2.

   *Whether The National Archives searched for the named corporate bodies,
   court proceedings and application references identified in my request*,
   rather than only searching the property names.
   3.

   *Whether The National Archives holds any recorded transfer, accession,
   disposal, destruction or retention information* indicating that records
   concerning the relevant property, estate, companies, litigation or
   government involvement were transferred elsewhere, destroyed, or otherwise
   disposed of.
   4.

   If such information is not held, *whether this is because no such
   records are held, because no relevant records were ever transferred to TNA,
   or because TNA's catalogue/search systems contain no discoverable
   description of them.*
   5.

   Whether *HMC9/311* or related series have been checked, or whether that
   reference falls outside the search undertaken.
   6.

   Whether there are *central-government, court, departmental or
   administrative records relating to the litigation and entities identified
   above which may contain references to the property without using “Great
   House Farm”, “Ty Mawr”, “Llandough” or “Cedfin” in the catalogue
   description.*

For the avoidance of doubt, I am not asking The National Archives to infer
the contents of uncatalogued records or to undertake an unlimited research
project. I am asking for confirmation of the *recorded information held by
TNA concerning the existence, provenance, transfer, retention, destruction
or disposal of potentially relevant records*, and for the searches
undertaken to locate that information.

That distinction is particularly important because a catalogue search
returning no result is not equivalent to a finding that no relevant
historical, governmental or archival records existed.

I would therefore be grateful if this could be reconsidered as a response

Thank you for your email regarding Councillor George Carroll and for setting out the background to your concerns relating to Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, now Church View Close.

Having reviewed your complaint, I do not consider that it falls within the scope of the Vale of Glamorgan Council's Corporate Concerns and Complaints Policy. The substance of your correspondence relates to historic planning, enforcement, land ownership, heritage and record keeping matters dating back several decades, together with requests for review, explanation and further investigation of those matters.
The Corporate Concerns and Complaints Policy is not intended to provide a mechanism for challenging or revisiting decisions where there is a separate statutory process or right of appeal; seeking changes to properly made decisions, policies or legislation; pursuing matters which are not the responsibility of the Council; promoting a particular cause or campaign; or addressing matters for which alternative legal or regulatory processes exist.
You have also requested that the matter be considered by me as the Monitoring Officer as a potential breach of the Member’s Code of Conduct by Councillor Carroll.
The role of the Monitoring Officer in this context is limited to considering whether there is evidence that a member has failed to comply with the statutory Members’s Code of Conduct. Having reviewed the information you have provided, I have not identified evidence which would indicate a breach of the Members Code of Conduct.
Accordingly, the issues raised will not be progressed under the Council's Corporate Concerns and Complaints Policy as they fall outside the scope of that procedure. Dear Mr Buckler,

Thank you for your further correspondence and for clarifying the purpose of your submission.

I understand the distinction you draw between seeking a review of the original 1988 decision and raising broader concerns about record-keeping, archival practice, and public accountability. However, the Committee's role is to scrutinise and hold the Welsh Government and associated public bodies to account in relation to policy, governance, and the use of public resources.

While I appreciate the broader administrative concerns you have identified, the issues raised in your correspondence arise from a specific historical case. The Committee does not have a role in reviewing or overseeing day-to-day operational decisions taken in individual cases. Accordingly, the Committee is unable to take forward the matters raised in your correspondence.

If you wish to pursue concerns regarding the management, retention or preservation of historical records, these matters are most appropriately raised with the relevant public authority or archival body responsible for those records. Similarly, concerns regarding the administration of a public body should be pursued through that body's complaints procedure and, where appropriate, with the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales.

Thank you for taking the time to write to the Committee and to set out your concerns in detail.

Yours sincerely,

Haidee

Subject: Re: Acknowledgement from the Culture, Communications, Cymraeg and Sport Committee


Dear Ms James,

Thank you for your considered response.

I understand and accept that the Committee does not have a remit to adjudicate upon an individual dispute, determine whether a historical decision was lawful, or direct Cadw to reopen a particular case. My submission was deliberately framed so as not to ask the Committee to do any of those things.

I would, however, respectfully clarify one point, because I am concerned that the nature of the request may have been characterised more narrowly than intended.

The attached report expressly states that it is not a legal challenge, a forensic proof of wrongdoing, a complaint seeking adjudication, or a demand for reversal of the 1988 decision. Its stated purpose is historical record correction, archival explanation and administrative acknowledgement. In particular, it asks for an explanation of why almost none of the records concerning the 1988 assessment survive, whether that reflects the applicable record-retention arrangements, and whether the surviving independent evidence should be properly reflected in the permanent public record.

The central issue therefore extends beyond the merits of the individual 1988 listing assessment.

Cadw's 2026 FOI response confirms that an assessment took place, but that only two exterior photographs now survive; the assessment report, reasons for refusal, site notes, internal recommendations and consultation correspondence are no longer available. The report does not assert that this proves wrongdoing. Rather, it identifies a straightforward public-administration question: how can the adequacy and evidential basis of an irreversible public heritage decision be understood or scrutinised when the underlying administrative record no longer survives?

That seems potentially relevant to the Committee's stated function of scrutinising the administration and accountability of Welsh Government and associated public bodies, even if the Committee cannot itself determine whether the 1988 decision was correct.

I am therefore not asking the Committee to investigate the Buckler family's historical dispute with BP, adjudicate upon the 1988 decision, or direct Cadw to reverse anything. The specific administrative questions raised in the report are instead:

  1.  What record-retention arrangements applied to the 1988 assessment?
  2.  Why do the assessment report, reasons, site notes and consultation records no longer survive?
  3.  Were the records destroyed under an applicable retention policy or other authority, and were they considered for transfer to the appropriate archival institution?
  4.  Is the present position consistent with Welsh Government/Cadw expectations for the preservation of records concerning significant heritage decisions?
  5.  Are current arrangements sufficient to ensure that comparable heritage assessments, particularly where a building is under imminent threat of demolition, are properly documented and retained?

These are not questions that require the Committee to determine the rights of either party to the original dispute. They concern administrative practice, institutional record-keeping and the ability of the Senedd and the public to scrutinise decisions taken by public bodies. The report specifically asks Cadw to explain the archival position and review its current record-keeping practices for this reason.

I would therefore be grateful if the Committee could reconsider whether the broader administrative and accountability issue falls within its scrutiny function, even if the Committee cannot examine the underlying individual dispute.

If the Committee considers that it nevertheless cannot engage with the matter, I would appreciate clarification as to which Senedd or Welsh Government scrutiny, oversight, archival or complaints mechanism is considered appropriate for raising a documented concern about the absence of the administrative record of a historical Cadw decision and the implications this has for public accountability.

For completeness, I should also emphasise that the report itself deliberately recognises the limits of the surviving evidence. It does not claim that Cadw acted unlawfully or in bad faith, and it expressly acknowledges that the absence of the 1988 working papers means that the assessment cannot now be reconstructed definitively.

My objective is therefore quite limited: to ensure that the surviving evidence is preserved, that the archival gap is properly explained, and that the public record accurately distinguishes what is established from what can no longer be verified.

I hope that clarification assists, and I would be grateful if you could confirm whether the Committee is able to consider the matter from that wider public-administration and accountability perspective.

Kind regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret’d Sergeant)
Royal Signals Cyber & Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

  *   Great House Farm / Ty Mawr and its farmhouse, garden or curtilage;

  *   any person other than the applicant asserting ownership or another interest in the land;

  *   possession proceedings concerning the farmhouse or land; or

  *   any objection, dispute, question or doubt concerning title.
